extracted.intended_audience: fans and readers interested in shojo manga art, fashion, and visual history; aspiring manga artists and commentators
extracted.subtask_description: A fan-blog overview identifying recurring visual and fashion features in shojo manga across the 1970s–1990s and how those features mark decades, artists, and emotional expression. Useful for readers comparing eras or for artists studying era-specific aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Western and historical makeup influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan was open to western beauty standards; makeup trends from the 1920s–early 70s show clear western influence, shifting later toward unique Japanese trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites Shiseido's overview of makeup history and suggests that illustrators imitated contemporary real-life makeup (e.g., eyebrow shapes, eye makeup). Use the historical timeline to explain why certain manga looks echo western icons like Audrey Hepburn in earlier decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary colors of traditional Japanese makeup
rubrics_metrics.description: Shiseido's 'primary colors of traditional Japanese makeup' — red lips, pale white skin and black eye lines — are visually echoed in illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating colored or cover art, check for these color cues (lipstick/blush emphasis, pale skin tones, defined black eye lines) as indicators of tradition-influenced styling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large eyes and small mouths as symbolic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists like Jun'ichi Nakahara drew big glassy doll-like eyes and tiny mouths 'because girls at the time were expected to be seen and not heard, so the large eyes symbolized their rich, unspoken inner lives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eye-to-mouth proportion is not just aesthetic but symbolic—large, expressive eyes imply inner life; tiny mouths imply silence/resignation. Use this to read character presentation and period sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of real-life eye makeup and eyebrow shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not realist overall, proportions (large eyes, tiny lips) coexist with eyebrow shapes and eye makeup that imitate how real women wore makeup at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess eyebrow shape and eyeliner/stylization as direct borrowings from contemporary beauty trends; these details anchor otherwise stylized faces to a real-world era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takarazuka Revue / theatrical makeup influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Takarazuka Revue's popularity influenced early shojo by emphasizing the eyes; stage makeup made eyes look bigger and more dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for theatrical exaggeration—heavy eye emphasis, dramatic lines—that mirrors stage aesthetics rather than everyday makeup, especially in early shojo illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye sparkles, shapes and their expressive uses
rubrics_metrics.description: 70s shojo eyes often look like 'windows' or 'galaxies' with sparkles in circles, squares and/or star shapes; some eyes are so sparkly they dominate the face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the shape and density of highlights (circular, square, star-shaped) as era markers and as tools for conveying innocence, wonder, or heightened emotion; different artists and decades prefer different sparkle motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic white/negative-space eyes for strong emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The 70s used dramatic white eyes to indicate strong emotions like shock; a star in one eye could denote being comically hit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify departures from detailed pupils (whiteouts, symbols) as shorthand for extreme emotional states; these are period- and genre-specific expressive conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyelash length and eyebrow thickness as decade markers
rubrics_metrics.description: 70s: thin eyebrows and very long eyelashes; 80s: eyelashes shorter and bushy eyebrows become common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare eyebrow and eyelash styling to date art—extremely long lashes and thin brows point to 70s aesthetics, while shorter lashes and thicker/bushy brows suggest the 80s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nose shape differences
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 70s, defined noses often look closer to a rectangle than a triangle; by the 80s/90s noses get softer and less rectangular when defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nose rendering (rectangular vs soft/triangular/minimal) as another stylistic clue when situating artwork temporally or stylistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mouth depiction and lip suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: 70s: full lips are suggested; 80s–90s: mouths often reduced to a thin line; many characters later show absence of lipstick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mouth detail (suggested full lips vs minimal lines) to infer era and whether color pages/cover art add makeup cues like lipstick or blush.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hairstyle volume, texture and shine as era indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: 70s: wavy hair and big ringlets; 80s: puffy, voluminous, wild-looking hair with little shine; 90s: smoother hair with lots of shine (except some grunge/dirty styles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hair silhouette (volume, ringlets, puffiness) and surface treatment (shine vs matte) are strong visual markers of decade; use them to distinguish 80s vs 90s aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body proportions and clothing silhouettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some decade trends elongate bodies (70s) while 80s bodies can look 'bulkier'; across decades bodies are usually thin and bust size generally small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how clothes interact with body proportions—pants, skirts, and fitted vs loose silhouettes—to read decade influences and how fashion alters perceived body shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion trends and color palettes across decades
rubrics_metrics.description: 80s colors more neon-ish; 90s colors calmer/darker. Fashion (e.g., bell-bottoms, European settings, grunge influences) helps date and style work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider clothing cuts, motifs (bell-bottoms, period dress, European fashions), and palette (neon vs muted) when situating art historically or narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist-specific stylistic range (simplified to realistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists like Katsuji Matsumoto ranged from simplified 'cartoony' styles (dots for eyes) to elaborate realistic renderings; stylistic range affects expression and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single 'era look'—check whether an artist is using a simplified or elaborate mode, and how that mode changes expressive tools (e.g., dot eyes vs full sparkles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution and conformity to contemporary trends over a series' run
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-running series/long-career artists sometimes change styles to conform to current trends, e.g., characters starting puffy/bulky and becoming slender/sleeker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a series, track visual changes over time—shifts in face shape, hair, fashion—attributed to trend adoption rather than just an individual artist's maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of makeup as characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Many girls are depicted as not wearing makeup (absence of lipstick is noticeable); colored pages and covers may add lipstick or blush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visible makeup (or lack thereof) to read character age, realism, or cover-specific glamor; absence of makeup can indicate intended innocence or everyday depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting influences on fashion choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of European settings in 70s works correlates with certain fashions appearing in illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor narrative setting (e.g., European locales) into fashion readings—setting can justify non-Japanese fashions or vintage looks within the same era.
